title: A strategic, systems-based approach to the management of land predators in Scotland
Biodiversity and soil health indicators to support high-integrity carbon credits in regenerative agriculture
Biodiversity Net Gain through nature restoration of urban green spaces
summary: Examines how restoring nature in urban green spaces in Glasgow and Aberdeen can deliver biodiversity gains and social benefits. Scotland's Biodiversity Strategy 2045 sets nature-positive goals and cities offer large scope for restoration, but measures such as reduced mowing and wildflower meadows can meet public resistance over untidiness. The work combines interviews and a photo-elicitation survey on local initiatives, analysis of existing biodiversity data from parks, and a multilevel statistical model linking ecological and social data to benefits, disbenefits and socio-demographic factors.

title: Bridging philosophy and ecology: ethical decision-making in wild salmonid conservation
summary: Wild salmonids such as Atlantic salmon and sea trout support Scotland's natural capital but face habitat loss, disease, climate change, pollution, overfishing and a possible threat from invasive pink salmon. Anglers, tourism operators, government and conservation charities hold goals that can conflict, for instance over stocking or eradicating invasive species. The project analyses these ethical trade-offs using philosophical methods, builds Bayesian hierarchical models that combine sparse high-quality monitoring data with biased angler records, and uses the models to predict outcomes of interventions, quantifying trade-offs under uncertainty for stakeholder feedback.

title: Bridging policy and practice: Marine Net Gain metrics for sedimentary blue carbon and biodiversity
Bundling benefits from peatlands to enable nature recovery
summary: Aims to design alternative ways to fund recovery of the UK's carbon-rich peatlands, focusing on bundled measures of ecosystem health and a range of public and private funding mechanisms. Voluntary carbon markets under the UK Peatland Code direct finance to measurable improvements, but full recovery needs longer-term attention to biodiversity. The work trials scalable monitoring methods, tracks how carbon emissions and biodiversity change across restoration stages at Corrour Estate, compares existing funding mechanisms, and designs an investment-ready package combining biodiversity and carbon gains.

title: Can Biodiversity Net Gain deliver positive outcomes for people and nature?
Capturing Biodiversity Net Gain on organic farms through citizen science
Distilling the value of nature: unlocking investment in nature-based solutions through integrated indicators for water, carbon and biodiversity
Finding the middle ground: balancing deer management, ecological recovery and traditional land use
Is 'complexity' the link between ecological function and the biodiversity metrics needed to deliver nature-positive outcomes?
Is there Net Gain in marine decommissioning? Rethinking the future and value of offshore infrastructure in the North Sea
The marine ecosystem net value of decommissioning offshore infrastructure: residual mercury contamination and the benefit of its removal
The marine rewilding effect: building a cost-effective framework for measuring Marine Net Gain
summary: Marine ecosystems underpin carbon storage and biodiversity yet face growing pressures, so restoration is urgent. Rewilding, which aims to build self-sustaining ecosystems, could deliver biodiversity net gain and social benefits, and nature markets may fund it, but reliable marine metrics are lacking. The project creates a scalable framework to monitor marine rewilding for these markets. Work includes acoustic indicators using Loch Craignish data, geospatial machine-learning indicators, societal indicators, and integration into the CreditNature platform with uncertainty reporting.

title: Meeting commitments to biodiversity conservation: a framework for predicting and monitoring the contributions of nature markets
summary: The Environment Act 2021 sets legally binding targets for England to halt the decline in species abundance by 2030, raise abundance by 2042 and improve the Red List Index. Nature markets, both compliance and voluntary, are central mechanisms, but their likely uptake and ecological effects are unknown. The project models plausible market scenarios and their effects on these indices, combining literature review, expert interviews, public surveys and quantitative modelling, and aims to produce a monitoring framework showing whether targets are on track and where new interventions will be needed.

title: Nature credits for oyster aquaculture
Nature markets and the future of crofting in the Western Isles
partners: Galson Estate Trust; Community Land Outer Hebrides

title: New nature markets at sea: evaluating stakeholder attitudes to guide policy and practice
summary: England plans a marine net gain scheme alongside land-based Biodiversity Net Gain, and a 2022 Defra consultation showed support for the principles but differing views on specifics. The project explores the perspectives of ecologists, policymakers, developers, NGOs, financiers and the public through workshops, focus groups and interviews. Stakeholder input is integrated into ecological models such as Ecopath with Ecosim and StrathE2E and compared with runs made without it. Modelled scenarios then return to stakeholders through spatial planning games and arts-based future-visioning workshops.

title: The potential for modern-day deer forests in facilitating and maintaining net gain in the uplands of the North Pennines
The potential for private investment in Biodiversity Net Gain and its ability to deliver Local Nature Recovery Strategies
partners: Natural England; Durham County Council; Durham Wildlife Trust
summary: Biodiversity Net Gain in England aims to compensate for development losses with a 10% uplift, relying on a biodiversity unit market expected to be largely privately supplied. The project examines whether private providers can enter this market and manage land profitably under different unit prices, using Durham Wildlife Trust as an example, and whether BNG can deliver Local Nature Recovery Strategies, checking through monitoring whether gains are equivalent for birds, butterflies and plants. County Durham is the case-study region.

title: Safeguarding genetic integrity: provenance-based seed sourcing to strengthen Biodiversity Net Gain
summary: Many nature markets measure biodiversity as habitat creation and often use mass-produced plant stock of unknown origin. Non-local stock risks genetic swamping of locally adapted populations. The project examines genetic variation among UK grassland wildflower populations with contrasting dispersal and pollination traits, comparing commercial seed with local and national genotypes, to define provenance zones for BNG planting. It then measures the social value of BNG habitats and of local versus non-local plants, working with Plantlife and other stakeholders to feed findings into future good practice.

title: Surveillance of the environment: monitoring ecological restoration and biodiversity in the Scottish uplands using uncrewed aerial vehicles
summary: UAV remote sensing could improve monitoring of biodiversity and carbon in the Scottish uplands, a contested landscape. The project develops new UAV methods and metrics to support evidence-based management, combines them with airborne and satellite data to monitor more widely and cheaply, and analyses the ethical, social and political implications of algorithmically processed environmental metrics. Challenges include calibrating UAV vegetation maps with field data, linking them to biodiversity standards, and addressing surveillance and democratic accountability.

title: Trading places: how market design shapes landscapes and biodiversity
Socio-economic and ecological factors for successful island restoration to deliver Biodiversity Net Gain across land and seascapes
summary: Eradicating invasive species, especially predatory mammals, is an effective way to restore islands, with benefits including seabird recovery, restored nutrient cycles and economic gains. Eradications on inhabited islands are difficult because they need community support. Using case studies such as the Channel Islands, the project runs qualitative and quantitative social science studies on stakeholder support and concerns, with discrete choice experiments identifying factors that shape acceptance. Outputs include a multidisciplinary toolkit for governments, NGOs, industry and communities.
